node.label: Romila Thapar
node.date_label: Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961) · From Lineage to State (1984) · Somanatha: The Many Voices of a History (2004) · The Past before Us (2013) · History as a Way of Remembering the Past (2014) · The Past as Present: Lahore keynote (2015)
node.description: A historian of early India who joined textual and material evidence to questions of social change. The Library of Congress’s 2008 assessment emphasizes that methodological shift. In her 2014 methods chapter she distinguishes historical consciousness from conformity to modern European genres. Her 2015 Lahore lecture challenges inherited religious divisions of Indian history and reconstructs the changing uses of the Somanatha narrative. Talbot’s review presents The Past before Us as a study of the social purposes served by perceptions of the past. These are distinct inquiries, not a claim that every premodern narrative is reliable history.

node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-24: the Library of Congress assessment; Thapar’s 2015 speech; her 2014 publisher excerpt at pp. 21–24; the displayed opening extracts of Talbot’s 2014 and Veluthat’s 2004 reviews. Books are unread; the 1961 and 1984 titles are catalogue-only. The 2015 speech is not the similarly titled 2014 essay collection. Later work and reception have not been surveyed; no career ending is asserted.

incident_edges.relationship: Thapar challenges colonial and religious-nationalist divisions of India’s past in her 2015 keynote
incident_edges.evidence_note: The speech criticizes the Hindu/Muslim partition of historical time inherited from James Mill and tests the Somanatha trauma narrative against differing sources. This targets specified narratives, not every national history.
